[p. 3] Validation of sports ‐related injury codes has shown ACL injury with the ICD ‐code S835E to have a positive predictive value of 96% [ 10]. DIF register All organized sport in Denmark is part of the Sports Confederation of Denmark (DIF), and since 2012, active athletes of the di ﬀerent sports are registered, divided by sport, sex and age. In Denmark, most sports are played in organized settings, except for activities like skiing, running, cycling, and swimming, where many recreational athletes are not members of a club or federation. However, to our knowledge, athletes participating in handball, football, basketball, volleyball, badminton, tennis and gymnastics are typically orga- nized in clubs and therefore registered, making it pos- sible to estimate sport ‐speciﬁc IRs when the injury activity is known. Sports chosen for analysis in this study were the ones reported with the highest rates in the DKRR. The register cohort (R ‐cohort) Patients aged 18 years and above at the time of reg- istration in DNPR with the ICD ‐codes S835 (lesion of the CL) and M235 (chronic instability of the knee) from 2000 to 2018 constitute the register cohort. The term nR‐cohort is used synonymously with the total number of patients registered in the R ‐cohort. Individuals could have been diagnosed with the above diagnosis more than once in the period; however, they appear only once in the R ‐cohort. Q‐cohort On 20 December 2021, all patients in the R ‐cohort who were still alive and registered as residing in Denmark were invited to answer a questionnaire through a per- sonal e‐mail sent through the national public digital mail solution, e‐boks. Patients who answered the ques- tionnaire constitute the Q ‐cohort (Figure 1). Based on the self ‐reported answers, patients with an injury date before 2000, who did not recall the injury date or had an injury date before the age of 18, were excluded and did not contribute data for analysis of IRs in the de ﬁned time period. The Q ‐cohort was divided into subgroups according to the patient's con ﬁrmation of diagnosis (Figure 1): patients with an ACL injury, patients with a bilateral ACL injury, patients with a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury, patients with CL injury without speciﬁcation, patients without a CL injury and patients not certain about having a CL ‐injury. The patients who had a bilateral injury or re ‐injury were instructed to answer the questionnaire regarding their primary injury. Patients reporting an ACL injury 

[p. 4] REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture) [ 11, 12]. If no response was registered, a reminder was auto- matically sent after 3 weeks via e‐boks. This was repeated up to three times. Study data were collected and managed using REDCap electronic data capture tools hosted at The Capital Region of Denmark. RED- Cap is a secure, web ‐based software platform designed to support data capture for research studies. The questionnaire consisted of three parts: (1) a general questionnaire collecting information about the injury and injury mechanism, (2) a questionnaire about return to sport and (3) the patient ‐reported outcome measures (PROMs): European Quality of Life —5 Domains (EQ. 5D), International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) [ 2, 31, 32 ]. The present paper presents data from the general questionnaire, including type of CL injury, site of injury (left/right), operative or non‐operative treatment, supervised physiotherapy, sport at time of injury, primary sport if any, and preinjury level of sport or activity (Supporting Information S1: Appendix A). The questionnaires were designed through repeated consensus meetings among the au- thors. The questionnaires were then tested on 10 pa- tients, and written feedback was obtained regarding the understanding of the questionnaire. Relevant adjust- ments were made, and the questionnaire was ﬁnally tested by 10 medical or physiotherapist research stu- dents regarding understanding, relevance, and time. Email: nckaldau@gmail.com Funding information Hvidovre Hospital; Badminton World Federation; Amager ‐Hvidovre Hospital Abstract Purpose: T o describe the epidemiology of adult anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures in Denmark from 2000 to 2018, focusing on: (1) overall ACL incidence rate (IR) per 100,000 inhabitants per year, (2) sports ‐speciﬁc ACL IR per 100,000 athletes per year and (3) ACL reconstruction (ACLR) IR per 100,000 inhabitants per year. Methods: This registry study utilized prospectively collected data from the Danish National Patient Registry (DNPR). Two ACL IRs were calculated: unadjusted IR based on registry data and adjusted IR corrected using patient self ‐reports to account for diagnostic misclassi ﬁcation. Sports ‐ speciﬁc ACL IRs (2012 –2018) were estimated by combining self ‐reported injury data with sports participation ﬁgures from the National Olympic Committee and Sports Confederation of Denmark. ACLR IRs were calcu- lated using procedure codes from DNPR, with annual Danish population data as denominators. Results: Between 2000 and 2018, 90,608 patients were identi ﬁed: 40,691 completed questionnaires. Overall adjusted ACL IR remained stable between 107/100,000 (con ﬁdence interval [CI]: 104 –111) in 2000 and 106/ 100,000 (CI: 103 –109) in 2018, increasing among females from 81/100,000 (CI: 78 –85) to 90/100,000 (CI: 87 –94) and decreasing among males from 134/100,000 (CI: 129 –140) to 122/100,000 (CI: 117 –127). ACLR IR rose from 36/100,000 (CI: 34 –38) to 43/100,000 (CI: 41 –45), with increases in both sexes, particularly among younger (18 –25 years) and older (>45 years) adults. Football was the leading cause of ACL injury overall and in men; women had more injuries in skiing and handball. The highest sports ‐ speciﬁc ACL IR was in female handball players, peaking at 2880/100,000 athletes in 2017. Females showed higher IRs in pivoting sports, while males had higher rates in gymnastics. Conclusions: While overall ACL IRs remained stable, an increase among females and a decline in males were found. ACLR rates have risen in both sexes. Female handball players had by far the highest ACL IR. MATERIALS AND METHODS This was a registry study from the DNPR with pro- spectively collected data on the cohort of interest. The study conformed to the Helsinki declaration, and ethical approval was not necessary since no intervention was performed. Approval to collect data was granted by the Danish Data Protection Agency (P ‐2020‐304). Two cohorts were formed: 1. The registry cohort (R ‐cohort) with all patients identiﬁed in the DNPR. 2. The questionnaire cohort (Q ‐cohort) with patients from the R‐cohort who responded to a questionnaire. Written consent from the participants in the Q‐cohort was obtained. T o estimate ACL and ACLR IR, the following reg- isters were used: The Civil Registration System (CRS), the DNPR and numbers from a register of active athletes in vari- ous sports in the National Olympic Committee and Sports Confederation of Denmark (DIF). CRS cohort All Danish residents are given a unique personal identiﬁcation (ID) number at birth or immigration via the CRS [29].
